1.pericope_label: I say the truth in Christ, I lie not: great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart

schools.summary: Gill explains why the profession is made at all: the apostle, being about to discourse concerning predestination, which he had mentioned in the preceding chapter, and to open the springs and causes of it, and also concerning the induration and rejection of the Jewish nation, thought it necessary to preface his account of these things with some strong assurances of his great attachment to that people and his affection for them, lest it should be thought he spoke out of prejudice to them; and he knew well in what situation he stood with them. On the sorrow he distinguishes the two words carefully: the one signifies grief, which had brought on heaviness of spirits, and the other such pain as a woman in travail feels. The trouble of his mind he describes by its quantity, that it was great and not a little but much, and by its quality, that it was internal and in his heart, not lying merely in outward show, so that neither the measure nor the sincerity of it can be questioned. Calvin says that in this chapter the apostle begins to remove the offences which might have diverted the minds of men from Christ, for the Jews, for whom he was appointed according to the covenant of the law, not only rejected him but regarded him with contempt and for the most part hated him. Hence one of two things seemed to follow, either that there was no truth in the divine promise, or that Jesus, whom Paul preached, was not the Lord’s anointed who had been especially promised to the Jews; and this twofold knot Paul fully unties in what follows. On the sorrow he observes that the apostle dexterously manages so to cut short his sentence as not yet to express what he was going to say, for it was not as yet seasonable openly to mention the destruction of the Jewish nation; and he adds that he thus intimates a greater measure of sorrow, since imperfect sentences are for the most part full of pathos. The cause of the sorrow will presently be expressed, after his sincerity has been more fully testified; and Calvin notes that the perdition of the Jews caused very great anguish to Paul even though he knew that it happened through the will and providence of God, so that submission to the decree and grief at its execution stood together in him.

Henry says we have here the apostle’s solemn profession of a great concern for the nation and people of the Jews, that he was heartily troubled that so many of them were enemies to the gospel and out of the way of salvation, and that for this he had great heaviness and continual sorrow. Such a profession as this, he explains, was requisite to take off the odium which otherwise the apostle might have contracted by asserting and proving their rejection; and he draws from it a rule for all who must deliver unwelcome truth, that it is wisdom as much as may be to mollify those truths which sound harshly and seem unpleasant, since if you dip the nail in oil it will drive the better. He observes that the profession is made with unusual solemnity, an appeal to Christ, a denial of falsehood and a summoning of conscience under the Holy Ghost, and that this weight of asseveration is itself evidence how bitterly the apostle expected to be misunderstood. The sorrow he takes as continual in the sense of habitual rather than unbroken, a grief that returned whenever the subject was before him; and he notes that it was sorrow for others and not for himself, which is the mark of a truly public spirit, since a man may be full of joy in his own case and yet carry a heavy heart for the condition of his people.

Clarke prefixes to the chapter an analysis of its argument: Paul expresses his great sorrow for the unbelief and obstinacy of the Jews, enumerates their high privileges, points out the manner in which God has chosen to communicate the knowledge of his name to both Jews and Gentiles, and shows how he deals, whether in judgment or in mercy, with individuals, producing the cases of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Esau and Pharaoh. God shows mercy and judgment as he thinks proper, and none have a right to find fault with his proceedings, since he has the same power over the human race as the potter has over the clay; and Clarke traces the rest of the chapter through the calling of the Gentiles and the stumbling of Israel at the stumbling-stone. Wesley states the purpose of the opening profession in a sentence: by declaring his sorrow for the unbelieving Jews, who excluded themselves from all the blessings he had just enumerated, the apostle shows that what he was now about to speak he did not speak from any prejudice to them. On the sorrow itself he draws a distinction that governs his whole reading of the passage, that a high degree of spiritual sorrow and of spiritual joy may consist together in the same man at the same time, as the close of the preceding chapter and the opening of this one show side by side.

Barnes says the chapter opens in some degree a new train of thought and argumentation, and that its main design probably was to meet objections which would be alleged against the positions advanced and defended in the previous parts of the epistle, where Paul had maintained that the barrier between Jews and Gentiles had been removed, that the Jews could not be saved by any external advantages they possessed, that all were alike guilty before God, and that there was but one way of salvation for Jews and Gentiles alike. On the sorrow he insists that the word rendered continual must be taken in a popular sense: not that the apostle was literally all the time pressed down with this sorrow, but that whenever he thought on this subject he had great grief, as we say of a painful subject that it is a source of constant pain; and the cause of the grief, though not expressly mentioned, is implied in what follows, namely that so large a part of the nation would be rejected and cast off. Ellicott paraphrases the first clause as meaning, from the bottom of my soul, in the most sacred part of my being, as a Christian man united to Christ, I make this solemn asseveration. The word conscience he takes here, as in an earlier chapter, very much in the modern sense of the word, namely the introspective faculty which sits in judgment upon actions and assigns to them their moral qualities of praise or blame; and the addition about the Holy Spirit he paraphrases as meaning that this conscience of mine is also overshadowed with the Holy Spirit and therefore incapable of falsehood or self-deception. Robertson counts the form of the oath precisely, observing that the apostle really takes a triple oath here, so strongly is he stirred: a positive affirmation in Christ, a negative one in denying that he lies, and the appeal to his conscience as co-witness in the Holy Spirit, the participle standing in a genitive absolute. On the sorrow he identifies its cause as the rejection of Christ the Messiah by the Jews, and quotes Sanday and Headlam that we may compare the grief of a Jew writing after the fall of Jerusalem. The word for consuming grief he calls an old word occurring in the New Testament only here and in the first letter to Timothy, and the adjective for unceasing a late and rare one, found in an inscription of the first century before Christ and in the New Testament only here and in the second letter to Timothy; two rare words standing together, both confined to this passage and the Pastorals, which he offers as some small argument for the Pauline authorship of those epistles.

Chrysostom opens his homily on the passage by comparing it with what he had preached the day before. Did I not seem yesterday, he asks, to have spoken some great and exorbitant things of Paul’s love toward Christ? And great indeed they were, too great for any words to express. Yet what you have heard today is as far above those things as those things were above ours; and though he had not thought they could be exceeded, when he came to what was read that day it did appear far more glorious than the whole of the former. He adds that the apostle was himself aware of this, and shows it by his exordium, since a man does not preface an ordinary statement with an oath, and the very solemnity of the opening is a measure of what is to follow. Theodoret takes the same clause more soberly and states what it accomplishes: the apostle proves that what he was about to say should be free from all falsehood and dignified with perfect truth, for he calls the grace of the Holy Spirit to witness with his conscience, in every way persuading his readers not to disbelieve his account. On the sorrow he observes that the composition of the sentence is incomplete, for it should have been added that the continual sorrow was caused by the rejection, or the infidelity, of the Jews; but through caution the apostle omits these distinct words and is content to teach in the sequel that he so meant, so that the broken construction is a piece of deliberate reserve rather than a lapse.

debates: Why the profession is made with so much solemnity: Gill says it was to prevent the suspicion that he spoke out of prejudice, since he was about to open the causes of predestination and the rejection of his own nation; Henry that it was requisite to take off the odium of asserting that rejection, adding that truths which sound harshly should be mollified as a nail is dipped in oil; Wesley that it shows he spoke from no prejudice; while Chrysostom takes the very solemnity of the exordium as the apostle’s own measure of what he is about to say

Whether the sorrow was literally unceasing: Barnes insists the word must be taken in a popular sense, since the apostle was not always pressed down by it but grieved whenever the subject was before him, while Wesley holds that a high degree of spiritual sorrow and of spiritual joy may consist together in the same man

Why the sentence breaks off unfinished: Calvin says the apostle deliberately cuts it short because it was not yet seasonable to mention the destruction of the Jewish nation, and that imperfect sentences are for the most part full of pathos, while Theodoret independently observes the same incompleteness and ascribes it to caution, the cause of the sorrow being taught in the sequel instead
outliers: Robertson counts a triple oath, positive, negative and by appeal to conscience
Robertson finds two rare words standing together, both otherwise confined to the Pastoral Epistles, and offers this as a small argument for their Pauline authorship
Calvin observes that Paul grieved bitterly over what he knew to be the will and providence of God
Ellicott takes conscience here in very much the modern sense, as the faculty which sits in judgment upon actions

3.pericope_label: For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh

schools.summary: Gill sets out and then rejects the reading that makes this a past wish belonging to the apostle's unregenerate state, when as a persecutor he wished to be separated from Christ; his answer is that no man would swear so solemnly to the truth of an enmity which everybody already knew, so the wish must be a present one. Calvin takes the wish at full weight: the added word proves that eternal and not merely temporal death is meant, since to be separated from Christ is to be excluded from the hope of salvation, and it was proof of the most ardent love that the apostle did not hesitate to wish for himself the condemnation he saw impending over his nation. He answers the doubt whether such a wish was lawful by fixing the boundary of love at what conscience permits: if we love in God and not without his authority our love can never be too much, and the apostle, seeing his nation endued with so many divine benefits, loved the gifts in them and them for the gifts' sake, counting it a great evil that such gifts should perish. He adds that the ardour of such feeling sees nothing but its object, so that election was not weighed against the wish but simply passed by.

Barnes marshals three objections against reading the verb as a past wish: the design of the passage is to state present attachment and present willingness to suffer, the grammar gives not I did wish but I could desire, and the apostle never in fact wished to be devoted to destruction by the Messiah, since while persecuting he believed himself to be defending his nation's hopes against an impostor. Robertson settles the question on the form alone, an idiomatic imperfect meaning that he was on the point of wishing; the present indicative would be wrong to say, and the constructions with the particle would place the wish either out of reach or too remote, so that the apostle is shut up to the imperfect indicative. Ellicott renders it I could have wished, holds that the wish related to what was really impossible, and calls it a nobly generous impulse at which some weak minds have been shocked and out of which others have made sentimental capital; he also asks whether the intensity of the expression does not help us realise one aspect of the atonement in him who was made a curse for us.

Wesley says human words cannot fully describe the motions of souls that are full of God, and that in how high a sense the apostle wished this none can tell unless he had been asked and had resolved the question; he did not then consider himself at all, but only others and the glory of God, and though the thing could not be, the wish was pious and solid, carried with a tacit condition if it were right and possible. Clarke, paraphrasing with Taylor, reduces the sacrifice to exclusion from the visible Church, so that the apostle wishes the rejection which will fall on the nation might fall to his own share if by that they could be kept in it, and sets the wish beside Moses offering to be blotted out rather than see the people destroyed. He remarks that few passages in the New Testament have puzzled critics and commentators more, since every reader saw the perfect absurdity of a literal sense, no man in his right mind being able to wish himself lost in order to save another.

Theodoret settles the sense of the curse from usage rather than from feeling. The word carries two significations, since what is consecrated to God bears that name and so does what is separated from him; he shows the second meaning from the closing words of the letter to the Corinthians and the first from the devoting of Jericho, and from common custom, by which whatever is offered to God is so designated. Here the apostle uses it in the second sense, to manifest the feelings he entertained toward his brother Jews. Theodoret also notices the exact verb: the apostle says not that he could desire but that he could pray to be separated from Christ, and this on a condition, provided that they who are his kindred in the flesh, being united to Christ, should reap salvation. He adds that the emphatic even I myself is aptly introduced, recalling to their recollection what had just been stated of the apostle's love to Christ.

debates: Whether the wish is past or present: Gill states the past reading as one held by some and refuses it because the oath would then guarantee a notorious fact, Barnes refuses it on grammar and on the apostle's own belief while persecuting, and Robertson refuses it on the form of the verb alone, an imperfect meaning that he was on the point of wishing

In what sense the wish could be entertained at all: Calvin defends it by the rule that love proceeds as far as conscience permits and by observing that ardent feeling regards only its object, Wesley by a tacit condition if it were right and possible, and Clarke by narrowing the loss to exclusion from the visible Church rather than from salvation

What anathema denotes here: Theodoret distinguishes the consecrated from the separated sense and assigns this place to the second, while Calvin insists the word carries eternal and not merely temporal death
outliers: Ellicott finds in the intensity of the wish an illustration of one aspect of the atonement, noting that the Greek word for curse in that other place is different though nearly equivalent
Theodoret observes that the apostle says he could pray, not merely that he could desire
Clarke reports that Wakefield saw no method of solving the difficulty of the verse at all

4.pericope_label: Israelites: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the law, the service, the promises, the fathers, and Christ according to the flesh

schools.summary: Gill notes that Israelite was the national name, taken from Jacob and accounted very honourable, and that the very name they bore gave the apostle concern that such a people should be cut off; the fathers are Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Calvin explains the grammar and the purpose together: the relative pronoun is put here in place of a causative adverb, so that the reason for the apostle's anguish is now plainly given, namely that they were Israelites, and to his kind feeling he adds other reasons of a higher kind, since the Lord had by a kind of privilege so raised them that they were separated from the common order of men. These titles of dignity were testimonies of love, for we are not wont to speak so favourably except of those we love; and though by ingratitude they rendered themselves unworthy to be esteemed on account of these gifts, the apostle continued justly to respect them, teaching us that the ungodly cannot so contaminate the good endowments of God but that they always deserve to be praised, while those who abuse them acquire thereby only the greater guilt. Calvin adds that descent from saints matters, since God promised the godly fathers mercy toward their children, though separated from the fear of God it is vain, and that the crowning privilege is that Christ proceeded from them.

Barnes reads the list as elevated external privilege: the adoption of the nation into the family of God, the glory as the symbol of the divine presence that attended them from Egypt and finally rested over the ark, the covenants as the compacts made from time to time with the patriarchs and the nation, the service as the temple service which they counted the ornament of their nation, and the promises as those of the Messiah. He treats the closing words as an appellation belonging only to the true God, remarks that there are no various readings of any consequence, and holds that the connection requires them of a nature not according to the flesh. Robertson explains the relative as meaning the very ones who, inasmuch as they, notes that the covenants are plural because renewed often, that the word for the giving of the law occurs only here in the New Testament, and that the punctuation which reads the doxology of Christ is the natural and obvious one, a full stop before it being abrupt and awkward. Ellicott names the glory the Shechinah, denies that the covenants are the two tables of stone, and weighs the doxology question at length on word order and context, having set prepossessions aside.

Clarke dwells on the dignity of the name, since Israel means a prince of God, so that the very name implied that they were a royal nation, princes of the most high God; he dates the adoption from the covenant made at Horeb, describes the glory as the manifestation of God among them in the cloud and the pillar and the presence between the cherubim, peculiar to the Jews and granted to no other nation, and reports that some suppose the singular put for the plural in the covenants and the decalogue intended. He calls the fathers without controversy the greatest men that ever flourished, and finds in the closing words a distinct statement of the twofold nature of our Lord, his eternal Godhead and his humanity. Wesley numbers six prerogatives whose pairs respect the Father, Christ and the Holy Spirit, holds that the covenant was given long before the law and is plural because so often repeated and because it had two dispositions, one promising and the other exhibiting the promise, and denies that the glory means the ark or any corporeal thing, since God himself is the glory of his people; the closing words he takes to imply the self-existent Being who was and is and is to come.

Theodoret takes the privileges one at a time and attaches a proof to each. The name was most celebrated, imposed by God himself on their forefather and transmitted as an heirloom to his descendants. The adoption they had obtained, as appears from the word that Israel is my son, my firstborn. The glory belonged to them because they had been illustrious through miracles. The covenants are not the old only, for he had promised to bestow the new upon them as well, saying that he would make a new covenant with the house of Israel not according to the covenant made with their fathers, but this they themselves were not willing to accept. The giving of the law is theirs because to them he had given the Mosaic law, and the service of God because, honouring them above other nations, he had taught them the ritual ministrations of the law. The promises are both those made by God to their fathers and those promulged by the prophets.

debates: Whether the glory means the visible symbol or God himself: Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Clarke all take it as the Shechinah, the presence that attended the nation from Egypt and rested over the ark, while Wesley denies that the apostle speaks here of the ark or any corporeal thing and holds that God himself is the glory of his people, adoption and glory being relative terms

What the plural covenants covers: Ellicott says not the two tables of stone but the several compacts made with Abraham and his descendants, Robertson that the plural stands because the covenant was renewed again and again, Wesley that it is plural because so often repeated and because it had two dispositions, while Clarke reports the view that the singular is put for the plural and the decalogue meant

How the closing words are to be punctuated: Ellicott lays out both readings as possible and decides for the application to Christ on word order and context, Robertson calls that punctuation the natural and obvious one, Barnes and Clarke and Wesley all read it of Christ's deity
outliers: Gill says the very name Israelite gave the apostle concern that such a people should be cut off
Wesley arranges the six prerogatives in pairs answering to Father, Son and Holy Spirit
Calvin holds that the ungodly cannot contaminate God's gifts, which still deserve praise while their abusers incur the greater guilt
Ellicott insists that prepossessions of every kind be set aside, since meaning is to be elicited from Scripture and not read into it

6.pericope_label: Not all Israel are of Israel: in Isaac shall thy seed be called; the children of the promise are counted for the seed

schools.summary: Gill says the apostle speaks thus partly to relieve his own mind and partly to prevent a mistake, since whether the word of God means the prophecies of the Old Testament, now about to have their accomplishment in the rejection of the Jews and the conversion of the Gentiles, or the gospel, which had had its effect upon the chosen ones among that people, it had not fallen; he notes how highly the Jews valued being the natural seed of Abraham, and that the birth of Isaac was the produce not of nature but of divine grace and power, typical of the regeneration of the elect. Calvin reads the verse as a deliberate recovery: having been carried by the ardour of his wish into an excess of feeling, the apostle returns to discharge his office as a teacher, restrains immoderate grief, and anticipates the inference that the covenant made with the seed of Abraham had failed. He holds that the hidden election of God overrules the outward calling and yet is not inconsistent with it but tends to its confirmation, and argues from the strongest case available, that if any natural progeny should have held, it was the first sons while Abraham lived and the promise was new.

Henry sets the verse in the argument as a whole: having made his way to what he had to say by a protestation of his affection and a concession of their undoubted privileges, the apostle now comes to prove that the rejection of the Jews by the establishment of the gospel dispensation did not at all invalidate the word of God's promise to the patriarchs, a suspicion which the present state of that nation naturally raised. He lays down the principle broadly, that we are not to ascribe inefficacy to any word of God, since nothing that he has spoken does or can fall to the ground; the promises and the threatenings alike shall have their accomplishment, and one way or another he will magnify the law and make it honourable. This is to be understood especially of the promise of God, which subsequent providences might seem to have defeated.

Robertson renders the paradox literally, that not all those out of Israel, the literal Jewish nation, are Israel, the spiritual one, and insists this startling saying is not a new idea with the apostle nor a clever dodge to escape a difficulty, since he had already shown elsewhere that those of faith are the true sons of Abraham; he notes that the seed here is physical descent while the seed of the following verse is spiritual, and that the quotation combines two passages. Barnes says not all the descendants of Jacob have the true spirit of Israelites, that the promise will not entirely fail, and that the distinction made between the two sons illustrated election at the very commencement of the nation's history, so that as God then rejected part of the natural descendants he might do so still. Ellicott observes a mixture of two constructions in the opening idiom, holds that the promise did not mean roundly all who could claim descent from Jacob, takes the seed as excluding the offspring of Hagar, and describes the children of promise as born through the miraculous agency of the promise, which is regarded as possessed of creative power.

Clarke states the Jewish objection in full, that God's faithfulness seems bound to continue the Jews as his peculiar Church notwithstanding the infidelity of the greater part, and answers that the whole body of natural born Jews are not the whole of the Israelites comprehended in the promise, since Abraham is the father of many nations and his seed is that of faith as well as that of the law. He presses the case of Ishmael, circumcised before Isaac was born and the son in whom Abraham desired the promise to be fulfilled, in whom God might have fulfilled it had he so pleased; and he warns that the apostle quotes only a hint of each passage, directing the reader to peruse the whole and there judge the argument. Wesley says the Jews imagined the word of God must fail if all their nation were not saved, and that the word itself had foretold their falling away; the sum of these chapters is that God accepts all believers and them only, which is no way contrary to his word, and Isaac was conceived by the power of the promise and not by the power of nature.

Cyril of Jerusalem supplies the pattern of faith that stands behind the argument. He offers Abraham as the one example from the older Scriptures that will serve, on the ground that we have been made his sons through faith, and says he was justified not only by works but also by faith, since though he did many things well he was never called the friend of God except when he believed, and his every work was performed in faith. Through faith he left his parents, his country and his home. Cyril then presses the birth itself as the test: in his body Abraham was already dead in regard to offspring and Sarah was old, so that no hope of children was left, and yet when God promised the old man a child he was not weakened in faith but, though he considered his own body as good as dead, heeded not the weakness of his body but the power of him who promised, counting him faithful. The exhortation drawn from it is that the hearer should be justified in the same manner.

debates: What the word of God here means: Gill allows either the prophecies of the Old Testament or the gospel and finds neither to have failed, Wesley takes it of the promises made to Israel, and Henry treats it as any word whatever of God, since nothing he has spoken can fall to the ground

How the promise is limited: Calvin holds that the hidden election overrules the outward calling while confirming it, Barnes that election was illustrated at the very commencement of the nation, Ellicott that the promise never meant roundly all who descended from Jacob, and Wesley that God accepts believers and them only

Why Ishmael is the decisive case: Clarke notes that he was circumcised before Isaac was born and was the son in whom Abraham himself desired the promise fulfilled, while Calvin argues that a separation made among the first sons, in Abraham's own lifetime and with the promise new, settles the question for the distant posterity
outliers: Robertson denies that the distinction between the two Israels is a clever dodge to escape a difficulty
Clarke warns that the apostle quotes only a hint of each passage and expects the whole context to be read
Ellicott describes the promise as possessed of creative power, the children being born through its miraculous agency
Calvin notes that the quotation follows the Hebrew rather than the Greek and traces the phrase at this time to a different passage than the one mainly followed

10.pericope_label: Rebecca conceiving by one: the elder shall serve the younger; Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated

schools.summary: Gill marks only that the case of the first two sons was not the only instance proving that Abraham's natural seed are not all children of God. Calvin carries the weight of the section. He observes that the sentence is again broken off before the principal verb, and that the second example is much more evident than the first, since some might allege inequality of condition where one was the son of a handmaid, whereas these were of the same mother and even twins, and yet one was rejected and the other chosen. He says the apostle now begins to ascend higher, to the cause of the difference, which is nowhere to be found except in the election of God, hitherto only obscurely hinted; now he openly ascribes the whole cause to an election gratuitous and in no way depending on men, so that in the salvation of the godly nothing higher is to be sought than the goodness of God, and in the perdition of the reprobate nothing higher than his just severity. He allows that the oracle concerned the right of primogeniture but insists it was the symbol of something greater, since Jacob gained little by it in the flesh, being driven from home, unkindly treated in exile, and prostrate in fear before his brother.

Barnes shows that the distinction is made on no natural principle: the younger was chosen and the elder rejected, though by the custom of the times the elder was entitled to peculiar honours. On the clause about the children he argues in numbered steps that they had done nothing good or bad, that where this is so there can properly be no moral character, that the period of moral agency had not begun, and that the purpose of God is therefore antecedent to any character in them. He reads the oracle of the posterities, the Edomites subject to the descendants of Jacob, and takes the prophet's hatred as no positive hatred but the withholding of privileges, love and hatred being used comparatively among the Hebrews. Robertson notes the idiom that the mother had a marriage bed of one husband, one father and twins, parses the two genitive absolutes, glosses the purpose according to election from the verb to select, and says not of works means not of merit, the source of the selection being God who calls. He admits the prophet's word sounds harsh, notes that the verb elsewhere falls short of hatred as we mean it, and hesitates to read the later enmity of the two peoples into it. Ellicott records the ambiguity of elder and greater in Greek and Hebrew alike.

Clarke frames the passage as answering a further Jewish evasion, that Ishmael was set aside not by God's sovereign will but as the son of the bondwoman; the case of Rebecca removes that plea, since the oracle came about two nations in one womb. He insists throughout on the national sense: the word children is not in the text and nations would be more proper, and taken personally the words are not true, for Jacob never exercised power over Esau but was subject to him and sorely afraid, acknowledging his brother to be his lord both by messengers and in person. The distinction therefore depends on nothing but God's free choice of a people to be the depositories of his especial blessings. Wesley agrees that the elder served the younger not in person but in his posterity, the Edomites being often brought into subjection by the Israelites, and that the words of Genesis and of Malachi agree. He holds that the choice was made before either had done good or evil, so that their ancestors were not accepted through any merit of their own, and that the saying relates neither to the persons of Jacob and Esau nor to the eternal state of them or their posterity.

debates: Whether the oracle is personal or national: Clarke argues at length that only the national sense can be true, since Jacob never ruled Esau but feared him and called him lord, Wesley and Barnes agree that the servitude was fulfilled in the posterities, while Calvin holds that the right of primogeniture was the symbol of something greater and that Jacob's earthly disadvantage proves it

How strong the prophet's word is: Barnes denies any positive hatred and takes the terms as a Hebrew comparative, Robertson notes that the verb elsewhere falls short of hatred as we use the word and hesitates to import the later enmity of the two nations, while Calvin reads the passage as showing that no privilege in the one brother accounts for the preference

What the pre-natal timing proves: Barnes concludes that no moral character yet existed and the purpose was therefore antecedent to it, Robertson that the phrase not of works means not of merit, Calvin that the whole cause lies in a gratuitous election, and Wesley that the ancestors were not accepted for merit of their own
outliers: Robertson explains the peculiar idiom by which the mother is said to have a marriage bed of one husband
Calvin observes that the apostle again breaks off before reaching the principal verb
Ellicott finds the same ambiguity between elder and greater in the Greek and in the Hebrew
Wesley denies that the passage touches the eternal state of either brother or of their descendants

14.pericope_label: Is there unrighteousness with God? I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy: not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth

schools.summary: Gill marks the opening words as the form the apostle uses when he is about to introduce an objection, and observes that the answer is built from testimonies out of the writings of Moses, whose name and writings were in great esteem with the Jews, so that full satisfaction might be given on both branches of predestination. He insists the closing inference is not a consequence forced by an adversary, as though men might sit still and do nothing and merely depend on mercy, but the apostle's own conclusion drawn from the cited testimony, and that what it concerns is election. Calvin warns that the flesh cannot hear this wisdom of God without being instantly disturbed by numberless questions and attempting to call God to account, predestination being in reality a labyrinth from which the mind of man can by no means extricate itself, while unreasonable curiosity grows the bolder as the examination grows more perilous. He renders the first verb as showing favour rather than mercy, following the Hebrew, and draws the inference that election is not to be ascribed to our diligence or striving or efforts but wholly to the counsel of God, who chooses those who neither will nor strive nor think of such a thing; he expressly rejects the view that we have some power to strive which merely fails unless assisted.

Henry states the standing of the parties before answering the charge. Having asserted the true meaning of the promise, the apostle comes here to maintain and prove the absolute sovereignty of God in disposing of the children of men with reference to their eternal state; and God is here to be considered not as a rector and governor distributing rewards and punishments according to his revealed laws and covenants, but as an owner and benefactor, giving to the children of men such grace and favour as he has determined in and by his secret and eternal will and counsel. Two distinct favours fall under that determination, the favour of visible church membership and privileges, which is given to some peoples and denied to others, and the favour of effectual grace, which is given to some particular persons and denied to others. Henry treats this part of the discourse as an answer to two objections, of which the first is whether there is unrighteousness with God if he thus chooses some and refuses others in what looks to us an arbitrary manner.

Barnes states the charge plainly, that God does injustice, notes that it has often been brought against the doctrine here advanced, and says the apostle repels it by showing that the teaching is explicit in the older Scriptures and founded on equity and on just views of sovereignty. He makes much of the occasion of the quotation, since the words were spoken when God declared that he would make all his goodness pass before Moses, so that they were given not as a proof of stern and inexorable justice but as the highest demonstration of benevolence he thought proper to exhibit, and those who charge them as arbitrary are perverting what God offers as kindness. On the inference he guards the other side, denying that it means the saved do not choose eternal life or are brought in against their own choice, since the effect of the Spirit is to make a man willing in the day of his power; what is denied is that life is bestowed for any original willingness of the man's own. Ellicott takes the running for a metaphor from the foot races the apostle may have seen at Corinth, and Robertson notes the particle expecting a negative answer and the apostle's fondness for the figure of running.

Clarke answers the objection with a general principle, that whatever God does is right and he may dispense his blessings to whom and on what terms he pleases, since bestowing peculiar privileges unequally on those otherwise in equal circumstances is not thereby inconsistent with justice. He paraphrases the words to Moses as a warning against any claim of right: God will make such a display of his perfections as shall convince that his nature is kind and beneficent, but he is a debtor to none of his creatures, his benefits proceed merely from his own good will, and no people, much less a rebellious people, can challenge them as due in justice or equity. He then finds the three terms of the inference illustrated in the history itself, since Abraham willed the blessing for Ishmael, Isaac designed it for his firstborn, and Esau ran a-hunting for venison that it might be regularly conveyed to him, and all alike were disappointed. Wesley makes the mercy consist with justice by holding that God has a right to fix the terms on which he will show mercy, and glosses the promise as mercy according to the terms he himself has fixed, on those who submit to them; the will of man is here opposed to the grace of God and man's running to the divine operation, and the declaration reaches all the spiritual children of Abraham to the end of the world.

debates: What the words to Moses secure: Barnes takes them as the demonstration of benevolence, spoken while God's goodness passed before Moses, Clarke as a denial that any creature can claim a debt, Calvin as favour shown according to God's own good pleasure, while Wesley reads them as mercy on the terms God himself has fixed, extended to those who submit to them

Whether the closing inference leaves any room for human striving: Calvin denies it wholly and rejects the view that we have some power which merely fails without assistance, Gill denies that the inference is an adversary's, Barnes denies that it makes the saved unwilling and appeals to the Spirit making men willing in the day of his power, and Wesley opposes the will of man to grace and man's running to the divine operation

In what capacity God acts here: Henry insists he is to be considered not as a rector distributing rewards by revealed law but as an owner and benefactor disposing of grace by his secret counsel, while Clarke rests the answer on the general rule that whatever God does is right
outliers: Calvin calls predestination a labyrinth from which the mind of man cannot extricate itself
Ellicott suggests the figure of running was drawn from foot races the apostle may have watched at Corinth
Clarke traces the willing and the running to Abraham, Isaac and Esau in turn, all of them disappointed
Calvin distinguishes the two verbs, the first meaning to show favour and the second to pity

17.pericope_label: The Scripture saith unto Pharaoh: for this purpose have I raised thee up; therefore he hath mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardeneth

schools.summary: Gill notes that the Scripture saith is a Talmudic way of speaking, used when a point is proved from Scripture and equivalent to saying that the merciful God says; the testimony is produced in proof of the other branch of predestination, called reprobation, and to vindicate it from the charge of unrighteousness, the raising up being God's own act. Calvin says the apostle comes now to the second part, the rejection of the ungodly, and because there seems something more unreasonable in this he labours to make evident that God in rejecting whom he wills is not only irreprehensible but wonderful in his wisdom and justice; the connecting particle reaches back to the question whether there is unrighteousness with God, and might be rendered moreover. He reads the raising up as done to this end, that while the king obstinately strove to resist the power of God he might, being overcome and subdued, afford proof how invincible the arm of God is, which no human power can bear much less resist. On the conclusion he refuses every softening: the word applied to God in Scripture means not only permission, as some washy moderators would have it, but the operation of the wrath of God; it seems good to God to illuminate some that they may be saved and to blind others that they may perish, and beyond his will we are not allowed to proceed.

Barnes treats the case as one of the most extraordinary instances of hardness of heart that has ever occurred, brought in to show that God may pass by those to whom he does not choose to show mercy and place them in circumstances where their true character is developed, and he notes that the haughtiest monarch is thereby proved to be under control. On the verb he observes that the Greek means properly to excite, rouse or stir up, while the older margin reads made thee stand, that is, sustained thee. On the conclusion he bounds the hardening carefully: it means only what the case specifies, not the exerting of a positive influence but the leaving of a sinner to his own course, though it implies an act of sovereignty in not putting forth the influence by which he might have been saved, and why this is the apostle does not say. Ellicott renders the verb brought into the world and on to the scene of history, holds that God uses the wickedness of men to exhibit his power and justice, and observes that the older narrative lays the hardening to the man's own act, which may yet be part of the design of providence, since the divine decrees include human free will without destroying it, though how we cannot say. Robertson distinguishes the national election of the earlier verses from the individual election here, notes that the man hardened his own heart while God also gives men up, and that the verb is a physician's word.

Clarke sets the passage against the alternative that God might justly have suffered Israel to go on in sin until wisdom and justice were signalized in their destruction. He translates the raising up of the recovery from the plague of boils and blains, God having restored the king to health and respited his deserved destruction to a longer day, so that in his instance such a demonstration of power might be given in his final overthrow that all mankind should learn who is God, the righteous Judge of all the earth and the avenger of wickedness. On the conclusion he holds that God in perfect righteousness bestows his blessings on one part of mankind while suffering another to go on abusing his goodness and forbearance, hardening themselves in sin until a just and exemplary punishment comes, unless this be prevented by deep repentance and return to God. Wesley grounds the whole on God's indisputable right to reject those who will not accept the blessings on his own terms, takes the raising up of the making of a great and glorious king, and reads the saying with a condition, that unless the man repented this would surely be the consequence. He suggests further that God was resolved to show his power over the river, the insects, the animals, the meteors, the air and the sun, all worshipped by the Egyptians, and at once over all their gods by the stroke that slew the firstborn.

debates: What raised thee up means: Barnes gives the Greek sense of exciting or rousing and notes the older margin reading made thee stand, Clarke takes it of a recovery from the plague and a respite of deserved destruction, Ellicott of being brought into the world and on to the scene of history, Wesley of being made a great and glorious king, and Calvin of being sustained in order that his defeat might prove the arm of God invincible

How far the hardening is God's act: Calvin insists the word means not permission only but the operation of the wrath of God, Barnes limits it to leaving a sinner to his own course while conceding an act of sovereignty in withholding saving influence, Ellicott points to the narrative laying it to the man's own act and holds that the decrees include free will without destroying it, and Wesley makes it simply a leaving of men to the hardness of their own hearts

On what terms mercy is shown: Wesley says on God's own terms, namely to them that believe, and Clarke that the punishment may still be prevented by deep repentance, while Gill and Calvin refer the difference wholly to predestination
outliers: Gill identifies the Scripture saith as a Talmudic formula for proving a point from Scripture
Robertson observes that the earlier verses concern a national election while this one concerns individuals
Robertson notes that the verb for hardening is a physician's word used by Galen and Hippocrates and occurs nowhere else in this apostle
Wesley proposes that the plagues were aimed one by one at the objects of Egyptian worship

19.pericope_label: Why doth he yet find fault? Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Hath not the potter power over the clay?

schools.summary: Gill treats the question as the objection of an adversary and characterises it sharply: it is the objection of a mere natural man, of one given up to a reprobate mind, an insolent hardened sinner, discovering the enmity of the carnal mind against God, one of the high things that exalts itself against the knowledge of him, a stretching out of the hand against God and a running upon him upon the thick bosses of his bucklers, marked with ill nature and rudeness to the last degree. He denies that the apostle met an objection he could not answer, and shows that the reply proceeds first by reminding the objector what he is, man and not God, a creature and not the Creator, who must not expect his Maker to give account of his matters; and he takes the potter's power over clay he never made but only purchased as an argument much stronger in the case of God, who created the clay itself. Calvin says the flesh especially storms when it hears that they who perish were destined by God's will to destruction, and that the ungodly, not content with defending themselves, make God guilty in their stead and then grow indignant at his power; constrained to yield, they storm because they cannot resist. He renders the reply as asking who thou art that enterest into a dispute with God, and insists that the potter's right is not arbitrary power but a privilege justly belonging to the maker, since as the potter takes nothing from the clay whatever form he gives it, so God takes nothing from man in whatever condition he creates him.

Barnes calls this the standing objection against the doctrines of grace, made by sinners in all ages, and analyses its grounds: it rests on the difficulty of reconciling the purposes of God with the free agency of man, and it assumes what cannot be proved, that a plan or purpose of God must destroy that freedom. He answers the objection in two stages, first by asserting God's sovereign right and then by showing that his dealing proceeds on principles of justice and mercy, and he ranges the impiety of arraigning God under heads: man is a creature and it is improper he should arraign his Maker, and he is unqualified, a being just in the infancy of his existence and of limited and interested faculties, to sit in judgment on the Infinite Mind. He observes that the prophet's figure is immediately preceded by the declaration that our righteousnesses are as filthy rags, so that men who have no claim and no merit suffer no injustice if favours are bestowed elsewhere. Robertson traces the objector's move, picking up the admission about the hardening, notes that still argues a change of condition and that the verb for withstanding is perfect, remarks on the emphatic word order and the double compound verb meaning to answer to one's face, and says the right claimed is a right over men already sinners. Ellicott takes the reply as an appeal to the religious sense rather than a solution.

Clarke frames the objection as the Jew's, parallel to the earlier cavil about being judged a sinner when the truth of God abounds through one's lie: if the glory of God is so highly promoted by our obstinacy, and he suffers us to proceed in our hardness, why does he find fault or punish us for what accords with his good pleasure? He answers by turning the objector upon himself, bidding weak and ignorant man reflect that after abusing the grace of God and transgressing his laws he now cavils at his dispensations. On the potter he recalls the prophet's errand to the potter's house, where the marred vessel was made again another vessel as seemed good, and adds the shrewd remark that no potter will take pains to make a vessel merely that he may show he has power to dash it to pieces; he also quotes old John Goodwin, who scarcely knew any passage of Scripture more frequently abused than this. Wesley hears the objector's temper in the words themselves, the particle still expressing sour, morose murmuring, and the pronoun his expressing a surliness that will not deign to name God. He distinguishes two views of the divine right, God as Creator, Proprietor and Lord dispensing his gifts with perfect wisdom but by rules quite out of our sight, and God as moral Governor and Judge dealing with us by rules clearly revealed and perfectly known.

debates: Whether the potter figure actually answers the objection: Ellicott concedes that in strict logic it confirms rather than refutes it, since no one blames earthenware for being badly made, and calls the appearance of a flaw inseparable from our imperfect conceptions, while Barnes, Gill, Calvin and Robertson take the figure as establishing the creator's right outright

What the potter's power means: Calvin denies that it is arbitrary power and calls it a privilege justly belonging to the maker, who takes nothing away from the clay, Barnes grounds it on the depravity declared in the preceding verse of the prophet, Robertson on the fact that the men in question are already sinners, and Clarke on the observation that no potter makes a vessel merely to break it

How the reply is meant to work: Ellicott says it is not so much a solution of the intellectual difficulty as an appeal to the religious sense to prevent the question being raised, while Barnes and Gill treat it as a substantive argument from the creature's incapacity to judge
outliers: Wesley reads the objector's temper out of the particle still and the bare pronoun that will not name God
Gill describes the objection as a running upon God upon the thick bosses of his bucklers
Clarke quotes old John Goodwin that scarcely any passage of Scripture is more frequently abused than this one
Wesley divides the divine right into that of Proprietor, exercised by rules out of our sight, and that of Governor and Judge, exercised by rules clearly revealed

22.pericope_label: Vessels of wrath fitted to destruction and vessels of mercy afore prepared unto glory, even us whom he hath called, of the Jews and of the Gentiles

schools.summary: Gill insists that nothing in these verses relates to any act of God before time, all of that having been considered already, so that what is now described is his conduct in time both toward those he passes by and toward those he chooses. He takes the riches of glory for the perfections of God's nature, his love, grace and mercy, his wisdom, power, faithfulness, justice and holiness, all displayed in the salvation of his people, and then moves from election to calling as its fruit and evidence, holding that election may be known by calling as a cause is known by its effect, without any extraordinary revelation, so that a man satisfied of his calling ought to be equally satisfied of his election. Calvin gives this as a second answer, showing that although the counsel of God is in fact incomprehensible, his unblamable justice shines forth no less in the perdition of the reprobate than in the salvation of the elect; no reason is assigned why this man is chosen and that rejected, since the secret counsel of God was not meet to be subjected to human judgment. He holds that the mercy shown the elect is made the clearer by the ruin of the rest, from which they differ in nothing but their deliverance out of the same gulf, and by no merit of their own; and he draws the double conclusion that grace is neither confined to the Jewish nation nor tied to all Abraham's fleshly children.

Barnes reads the verse as the second stage of the answer, applied now to the two classes actually existing, the righteous and the wicked, and asks whether God in fact does wrong to either; on the willingness he replies that if a thing is right to do it is right to purpose to do it. He glosses the riches of glory as a Hebrew form meaning abundant glory, and distinguishes grace as favour to the undeserving from mercy as favour to the miserable; from the last verse he concludes both that grace was never confined to the Jewish people and that God was not bound to confer it on the whole mass of Abraham's descendants, since he took individuals out of the nations rather than nations as such. Robertson takes the first participle concessively, although willing, not causally, as the phrase about much long-suffering shows; on the second he notes a perfect passive denoting a state of readiness and remarks pointedly that the apostle does not say here either that God did it or that they did it, though responsibility appears elsewhere, and that the destruction meant is endless perdition and not annihilation. Ellicott finds the sentence grammatically incomplete at two points, ascribes the irregularity to dictation and the lively flow of thought, and identifies the vessels of glory as those meant to accept the Christian teaching, Jew or Gentile, the vessels of wrath being the unbelieving mass of Israel.

Clarke refers the passage first to Pharaoh and the Egyptians, persons deeply guilty who by obstinate refusal of grace and abuse of goodness had fitted themselves for the destruction which vindictive justice inflicted after much long-suffering, and calls this absolute proof that the hardening of their hearts and their ultimate punishment were the consequences of their own refusal. The Jews of the apostle's day had sinned after the similitude of the Egyptians and were ripe for the same. He adds a reason for the timing of their overthrow: they had been fitted for destruction long before, but the fittest season came only after the believing Gentiles had been prepared unto glory, since the Jewish nation was to supply the first preachers of the gospel and had to be preserved until that preaching had taken deep root in the Gentile world. Wesley reads the willing concessively, since although it was now God's will, because of their obstinate unbelief, to show wrath, which necessarily presupposes sin, he yet endured them as he endured Pharaoh with a long-suffering that should have led them to repentance; the vessels of wrath are those who had moved his wrath by still rejecting his mercy, and they were fitted for destruction by their own wilful and final impenitence. He then marks the turn to grace free for all, whether Jew or Gentile.

debates: Who does the fitting: Clarke and Wesley both make the vessels of wrath fit themselves, by obstinate refusal of grace and by wilful final impenitence, whereas Robertson observes that the participle is passive and that the apostle does not say here either that God did it or that they did it, and Calvin refers the whole difference to a secret counsel which no reason of ours may examine

Why the sentence is left unfinished: Ellicott finds two grammatical suppressions and ascribes them to the apostle's habit of dictating and the lively flow of his thought, while Calvin supplies the missing clause as a question asking who can charge God with unrighteousness

How the long-suffering is to be read: Robertson and Wesley take the participle concessively, so that God bore with the vessels of wrath although willing to show wrath, and Ellicott adds that he gave them time for repentance, while Barnes rests on the rule that what is right to do is right to purpose
outliers: Robertson insists that the destruction spoken of is endless perdition and not annihilation
Gill argues that election may be known by calling as a cause is known by its effect, without extraordinary revelation
Clarke explains the delay of the Jewish overthrow by the need to preserve that nation until the gospel had rooted among the Gentiles
Barnes distinguishes grace as favour to the undeserving from mercy as favour to the miserable

25.pericope_label: As he saith also in Osee: I will call them my people which were not my people, and her beloved which was not beloved

schools.summary: Gill notes that the form Osee stands for Hosea as in the Greek version, that the prophecy speaks of the calling of the Gentiles as the spiritual Israel after God had written lo-ammi and lo-ruhamah upon the Jewish people, and that the foretelling of their calling long before they were in being could have no other foundation than his own eternal sovereign will and pleasure; on the second citation he takes the place named strictly, as the very selfsame spot of ground in the countries concerned. Calvin faces the difficulty of the application squarely: no one can deny that the prophet in that passage speaks of the Israelites, whom the Lord, offended with their wickedness, declared should be no longer his people, and to whom he then subjoined the consolation that of those not beloved he would make some beloved; yet the apostle applies to the Gentiles what was expressly spoken to the Israelites. He reports the solution of those who have been most successful in untying the knot, that what might hinder the Gentiles existed in the Jewish nation too. On the word beloved he holds that those are said not to be beloved to whom God declares wrath rather than love, and that although they whom God has destined as sons are perpetually his sons, Scripture in many places counts none his children except those whose election has been proved by their calling, so that we are not to judge of election but as it manifests itself by its own evidences.

Henry explains why the prophets are produced here at all. Having explained the promise and proved the divine sovereignty, the apostle now shows how the rejection of the Jews and the taking in of the Gentiles were foretold in the Old Testament, and therefore must be very well consistent with the promise made to the fathers under that Testament; it tends very much to the clearing of a truth to observe how the Scripture is fulfilled in it, and the Jews would no doubt willingly refer the matter to writings that had been committed to themselves, so that what was uneasy to them is shown to have been spoken of there. On the first prophecy he dwells on the greatness of the change: the Gentiles had not been the people of God, neither owning him nor owned by him in that relation, and now he says he will call them his people, make them such and own them as such, notwithstanding all their unworthiness, which he calls a blessed change and takes as proof that former badness is no bar to God's present grace and mercy. Those whom God calls his people he also calls beloved.

Barnes sets out the three points the quotations are brought to confirm, that God intended to call his people from the Gentiles as well as the Jews, that he was bound by no promise or principle of obligation to bestow salvation on all the Jews, and that it was therefore right for him to cut off any of them from their privileges as a people. He grants that the words in the prophet did not refer to the calling of the Gentiles but to the recalling of rejected Jews, and argues that if God formerly purposed to recall a people he had rejected and to bestow favours after they had been forfeited, the same dealing is not to be thought absurd toward the Gentiles, who are also part of the original family of man. Ellicott says the original prophecy relates to the pardon and reconciliation promised the apostate northern kingdom and is here typically and prophetically applied, since those who had ceased to belong to the chosen people and those who had never belonged to it were to all intents in the same position; he quotes Lightfoot on the pronunciation of the prophet's name and records a doubt whether the Hebrew of the second citation should be rendered instead of calling them. Robertson notes that the prophet speaks of the ten tribes while the apostle applies the principle, that the phrases were the names of the prophet's own children, and that the place named was Palestine in the original.

Clarke complains that no uniformity in the orthography of proper names has been preserved between the two Testaments, and asks what stranger to our sacred books would suppose that the form used here meant the prophet Hosea. He insists that the calling of the Gentiles was no fortuitous thing but a firm purpose in the divine mind, largely revealed to the prophets, so that by opposing that calling the Jews in effect renounced their own prophets and fought against God. Reading the two citations together, he takes the decrease of the Church by the utter taking away of the ten tribes to be well supplied afterwards by the calling in of the Gentiles: they who had been the people of God should become not my people, while they who had been not my people should become the children of the living God. Wesley glosses beloved as a spouse, and draws from the words her beloved which was not beloved the inference that such a one was consequently not unconditionally elected, referring the passage directly to the final restoration of the Jews; on the second citation he observes that they shall be called sons of God in the very place where they are, so that they need not leave their own country and come to Judea.

debates: How a prophecy spoken to Israel can be applied to the Gentiles: Calvin admits the words plainly concern the Israelites and reports the argument from the greater case to the less, Barnes reasons that recalling a rejected people makes the calling of another no absurdity, Ellicott treats the application as typical and prophetical, and Robertson says the apostle applies the principle rather than the reference

What the phrase not beloved proves: Wesley infers from it that such a one was not unconditionally elected and reads the passage of the final restoration of the Jews, while Calvin takes it of those to whom God declares wrath rather than love and uses it to argue that election is known only as it manifests itself in calling

Where the promised naming takes place: Robertson says the original meant Palestine and is applied to scattered Jews and Gentiles everywhere, Wesley that they need not leave their own country for Judea, Gill that it is the very selfsame spot of ground, while Ellicott records a rendering that removes the place altogether
outliers: Clarke complains of the want of uniformity in spelling proper names between the two Testaments
Ellicott quotes Lightfoot on whether the prophet's name should be sounded as two syllables or three
Robertson observes that both phrases were the names given to the prophet's own children
Henry takes the change as proof that former badness is no bar to God's present grace and mercy

27.pericope_label: Esaias crieth concerning Israel: though the number be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved; except the Lord had left us a seed

schools.summary: Gill treats the introduction as significant, taking the prophet's crying either of the concern and sorrow with which he spoke, even with strong crying and tears, seeing that a remnant only was to be saved, or of his heart's desire and prayer for Israel, wrestling with God on their behalf; and he observes that these testimonies, while they prove the calling of some from among the Jews, at the same time suggest the casting off of the far greater number, which is the apostle's view in citing them. On the difficult following verse he canvasses and rejects several readings, that which makes it an account balanced so that little remains, that which takes the word of the incarnate Word cut off in a short time, that which applies it to the abolishing of the ceremonial law and the abridging of the moral, and that which finds the gospel righteousness in it, all of them foreign to the apostle's purpose. Calvin says the apostle proceeds now to the second part, with which he was unwilling to begin lest he exasperate their minds, and that the prophet is made to exclaim rather than to speak in order that more attention might be excited; the saying was meant to keep the Jews from glorying in the flesh, since it was dreadful to hear that of so vast a multitude only a small number should be saved. He applies the prophecy through the deliverance from Babylon, which was purposed for very few of that multitude.

Barnes observes that the doctrine of the rejection of the Jews was a far more difficult point to establish than the calling of the Gentiles and therefore needed fortifying by an explicit passage, and that although the prophet had reference primarily to the wicked generation of his own time, the case settled a general principle of the Jewish government and so applied to the apostle's argument. On the hard verse he notes that the Greek version and the apostle keep the sense but not the words of the Hebrew, that finishing the work means bringing the thing to an end and cutting it short means executing it speedily, so that the destruction shall not be delayed, and that it is done in righteousness, as an expression of God's abhorrence of the people's sins. He explains the divine title at length: the word means hosts, armies organised for war, and hence the angels marshalled in military orders and also the stars, God being their King and Commander. Ellicott presses the article, the remnant and only the remnant, notes that the original word means shall return, so that the apostle has put the consequence of conversion for the conversion itself, renders the next verse a short and summary sentence executed upon the earth, and takes its severity as proof that only a remnant can be saved. Robertson notes the textual variation in the noun for remnant, the two compounded participles, and the unfulfilled condition in the last citation.

Clarke states the object of the argument plainly, that God for their infidelity had rejected the great body of the Jews and that but a few of them would embrace the gospel and be saved from the destruction now coming to sweep away them and their state; and he sets beside it Taylor's paraphrase, that the taking of a small remnant into the Church now is agreeable to former dispensations. He calls the terms of the hard verse forensic, referring to the conclusion of a judicial proceeding in which the Lord has tried and found them guilty and will immediately execute the punishment due. On the last citation he observes that had not God in mercy preserved a very small remnant to keep up the name and being of the nation, it had been cut off and extinct like the cities of the plain, and that we thus learn it is no new thing with God to abandon the greater part of a corrupt Jewish nation and confine his favour to a believing few; the change from remnant to seed he takes as intimating that just enough of the righteous were left to be a seed for a future harvest of true believers. Wesley says that as many Gentiles will be accepted so many Jews will be rejected, that the word was spoken originally of the few saved from the ravage of an invading army, that in rigorous justice a small remnant only will be left, and that the seed denotes both the present paucity and the future abundance.

debates: What the crying signifies: Gill takes it of the prophet's own sorrow or of his intercession for Israel, Ellicott and Robertson of the impassioned anguish of his utterance, and Calvin of a deliberate contrivance to excite attention in the hearers

How the difficult verse is to be read: Gill rejects four current explanations as foreign to the purpose, Barnes takes the finishing and cutting short as speedy execution of a threatened destruction, Ellicott renders it a short and summary sentence, Clarke reads the terms as forensic, and Calvin makes the residue itself look like a consumption

What the remnant proves: Ellicott says that but for it the rejection would have been utter and complete, Clarke that just enough of the righteous were left to seed a future harvest, Wesley that the word marks present paucity and future abundance, while Gill and Calvin take the same testimonies as evidence of how few were to be saved
outliers: Ellicott notes that the prophet's book was already collected in the form we have it
Barnes derives the divine title from armies organised for war and applies it to the angels and to the stars alike
Calvin observes that the Greek version leaves this divine title untranslated here while rendering it variously elsewhere
Robertson records that the manuscripts differ over the very word for remnant

30.pericope_label: The Gentiles attained to righteousness which is of faith, but Israel, following after the law of righteousness, attained not, because they sought it not by faith

schools.summary: Gill treats the opening question as an invitation to object and an answer at once: the calling of a large number of Gentiles and very few Jews, according to God's eternal purposes, is chargeable with no unrighteousness but must be referred to his sovereign will and pleasure, and is an instance of grace and goodness, since all were so wicked that he might in justice have destroyed every individual. He describes the Jewish pursuit vividly, that they were zealous of what is called the law of righteousness because the matter of it was righteous and because perfect obedience to it is righteousness, and that they tugged and toiled and laboured with all their might, as men in a race, to come up to it. Their failure he lays to two errors, that they sought righteousness in the wrong object, in the law where a sinful creature can never find it and not in Christ, and in the wrong way, not by faith without which it is impossible to please God. Calvin says the apostle now begins to show those causes of the rejection which human minds can comprehend, while warning that it is absurd to set up any cause above the secret predestination of God, which is the first cause. He calls the Gentile case the more unreasonable in appearance, and says the Jews by running out of the way wearied themselves in vain; those who attempt salvation by trusting their own works are deservedly rejected, since so far as in them lies they abolish faith.

Henry says the apostle comes here at last to fix the true reason of the reception of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews. There was a difference in the way of their seeking, and therefore there was that different success, though still it was the free grace of God that made them differ; and he concludes like an orator, asking what shall we say then, what is the conclusion of the whole dispute. Of the Gentiles he observes first how they had been alienated from righteousness, since they followed not after it, knew not their guilt and misery, and were therefore not at all solicitous to procure a remedy. In their conversion preventing grace was greatly magnified, God being found of those who sought him not, and there was nothing in them to dispose them for such a favour more than what free grace itself wrought in them; thus God delights to dispense grace in a way of sovereignty and absolute dominion.

Barnes says the question is asked preparatory to summing up the argument, which had been so stated that the conclusion was inevitable, and notes that by the time of writing multitudes of the heathen had embraced the faith. He guards the statement about the Gentiles, denying that it means none of them had any solicitude about right and wrong or that no anxious inquiries were made among them, the point being to set them in contrast with the Jew. The law of righteousness he takes as the just law, which demands perfect purity even in its external observance, and which the Jews supposed they obeyed so as to constitute a meritorious ground of justification; their failure he refers back to the earlier chapters, where the law is shown to demand perfect compliance. He also meets the question how the Jews could have known any better, answering from the older Scriptures themselves and from the reference of the sacrifices to a future state of things. Robertson observes that the verb for attaining keeps up the figure of the chase, meaning to grasp or overtake, calls the result a curious paradox, and says that legal righteousness Israel failed to reach because reaching it required keeping the whole law perfectly. Ellicott notes that the Gentiles had no special revelation and were inattentive to the law of conscience, that Israel tried to keep the law but failed to come under its protection, and that a word is to be dropped from the text.

Clarke refers the reader back to his own long note on the opening of the epistle and contents himself with Taylor's paraphrase, in which the apostle, having vindicated the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles with regard to the divine veracity and justice, now turns to the true reason and state of the affair considered in itself. Of Israel he says that though they had been the people of God and were industrious in observing a rule by which they supposed they could secure the blessings of his peculiar kingdom, they never came up to the true and only rule by which those blessings can be secured. Their mistake he locates precisely: being ignorant of God's righteousness, that is, of his method of saving sinners by faith in Christ, they went about to establish their own method of obtaining salvation, attending not to the Abrahamic covenant, which stands on the extensive principles of grace and faith, but turning all their regard to the law of Moses, and imagining that obedience to it gave them a right to the blessings of the Messiah's kingdom; finding the gospel to set the matter on a different footing, they were offended and refused to come into it. Wesley draws the two conclusions in order and then asks whether the failure was because God eternally decreed they should not attain, answering that there is nothing like this to be met with, the reason assigned being that they sought it not by faith.

debates: Why Israel failed: Gill says they sought righteousness in the wrong object and the wrong way, Barnes that they depended on their own righteousness rather than on mercy, Clarke that they were ignorant of God's method and turned from the Abrahamic covenant to the law of Moses, Calvin that trust in works abolishes faith and would annihilate righteousness if it succeeded, while Wesley expressly denies that any eternal decree accounts for it

How far the causes given here reach: Calvin allows that the apostle is now showing causes which human minds can comprehend, but insists that it is absurd to set any cause above the secret predestination of God, whereas Henry, though ascribing the whole difference to free grace, rests the explanation on the difference in the way of seeking

What is meant by saying the Gentiles did not follow after righteousness: Barnes denies that it makes them wholly without solicitude about right and wrong, Ellicott explains it by their want of special revelation and inattention to conscience, Henry by their not knowing their own guilt and misery, and Calvin by their rolling themselves in the lasciviousness of the flesh
outliers: Gill pictures the Jews tugging and toiling like runners in a race to come up to the law
Robertson notes that the verb for attaining continues the figure of pursuit, meaning to overtake
Barnes answers the objection that the Jews could not have known of justification by faith, appealing to the older Scriptures and to the sacrifices
Ellicott records that the second occurrence of righteousness is absent from the best manuscripts

33.pericope_label: Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence: and whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed

schools.summary: Gill notes that the citation is drawn from two places, the beginning and end from the one and the middle from the other, and calls this an instance of skipping from place to place, concerning which the Jewish rules for reading laid down conditions. Calvin traces the same seams, observing that the opening words come from one prophecy, the stone of stumbling and rock of offence from another, and the closing promise again from the first, and calls the citation remarkable in its manner though the subject is one. He reads the last clause as consolation subjoined for the godly, as if the apostle had said that because Christ is called the stone of stumbling there is no reason we should dread him or entertain fear instead of confidence, since he is appointed for ruin to the unbelieving but for life and resurrection to the godly; as the former prophecy of stumbling is fulfilled in the rebellious and unbelieving, so this other is intended for the godly, that he is a firm stone, precious, a corner stone most firmly fixed, and whoever builds on it shall never fall.
