On the difference of the versions he holds that the Hebrew word will bear a similar meaning and may be rendered shall not hurry or be confounded, and that since the Lord in that place intended to strengthen the hope of his people, it follows that those who entertain good hope cannot be ashamed.

Barnes traces the name of the place through its senses, from the hill in Jerusalem over against the mount on which the temple was built, where the palace of David stood and the court resided, to the whole city, then to the capital and the glory of the people of God and the place of solemnities, and hence to the church itself, which is its meaning here. The application of the word rock he derives from the custom of building, the same one being the corner stone on which the church is reared, not on human merits but by the righteousness of the Saviour, so that the stone designed as a corner stone became by their wickedness the block over which they fell into ruin; and he insists that he is called a rock of stumbling not because it was the design of sending him that men should fall, but because such would be the result. On the last clause he explains that the Hebrew word means literally to make haste but also to be afraid, as one who makes haste often is, and so approaches the sense of shame, the promise being that the believer shall not be agitated by fear of failure nor disappointed of his hope. Ellicott calls the quotation a free combination, distinguishes the foundation stone of the temple in the one passage from God himself in the other, and defends the application of both to the Messiah. Robertson renders the phrase a rock of snare and notes the same combination elsewhere.

Clarke states plainly why the stone became an offence. The Messiah whom God would bring in was to be a widely different person from the one the Jews expected, for whereas they looked for a mighty secular prince who should set up a secular kingdom, he appeared a man of sorrows and acquainted with griefs, and redeemed mankind not by his sword or by secular power but by his humiliation, passion and death; therefore they were offended at him and rejected him, and thought it would be reproachful to trust in such a person for salvation. Against this he sets the promise: so far shall any be from confusion or disappointment who believes in Christ that on the contrary every genuine believer shall find salvation, the remission of sins here and eternal glory hereafter. Wesley reads the verse as foretold by their own prophet, and paraphrases the laying of the stone as God exhibiting in his church what, though it is in truth the only sure foundation of happiness, will in fact prove a stumbling stone and rock of offence, an occasion of ruin to many through their obstinate unbelief.

debates: How the two prophecies are to be taken together: Gill treats the joining as an instance of skipping between places, Calvin traces the seams clause by clause and calls the manner remarkable, and Ellicott distinguishes the original references, the temple foundation stone in one and God himself in the other, defending the application of both to the Messiah

Whether the stumbling was the purpose or the outcome: Barnes insists he is called a rock of stumbling not because it was the design of sending him that men should fall but because such would be the result, Wesley calls the same stone in truth the only sure foundation of happiness and in fact an occasion of ruin through obstinate unbelief, and Clarke lays the offence to the expectation of a secular prince

What the last clause promises: Ellicott and Robertson record only that the Hebrew reads shall not make haste, Barnes shows how that word approaches the sense of shame through the idea of fear, and Calvin argues from the prophet's purpose of strengthening hope that those who hope cannot be ashamed
outliers: Robertson infers from the same pair of quotations in another epistle either that one apostle had read the other or that both used a collection of testimonies
Barnes takes Zion here to mean the church itself, tracing the word through hill, city, capital and people
Clarke describes the expected Messiah as a mighty secular prince and contrasts him with the man of sorrows
Calvin notes that the apostle followed the Greek rendering in the closing clause
